Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

extent noun

how far something goes; the degree

also to what extent, to some extent, to a certain extent, to such an extent that, to the extent that, so far as, in so far as

classical

Cic. Lael. 61: est enim quātenus amīcitiae darī venia possit
Cic. de Or. 2.237: quātenus sint rīdicula tractanda ōrātōrī (Lewis & Short)

quātenus

adverb, in indirect questions; answered by eātenus, “so far”

how far, to what extent

Properly “up to where”. The answer is eātenus, “so far, to that extent”, with quoad or ut (Cic. Leg. 1.14, Lewis & Short). In Horace and later, quātenus also means “since, seeing that” (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • adeō … ut — to such an extent that, so … that

    adverb with a consecutive ut-clause (subjunctive) · classical · Hor. Ep. 1.1.39: nēmō adeō ferus est, ut nōn mītēscere possit; Cic. Fl. 47: nēminem quidem adeō īnfatuāre potuit, ut eī nummum ūllum crēderet (Lewis & Short)

    With verbs, adjectives and nouns, in every period (Lewis & Short); ūsque adeō is stronger, “so very much”.

  • 1Lewis & Short cites the passage as Sen. Ep. 116, 4; in the Perseus text it stands in section 3, which we follow.

    aliquātenus1 — to some extent, in some measure

    adverb · also used · post-classical · Sen. Ep. 116.3: aliquātenus, inquis, dolēre, aliquātenus timēre permitte; Quint. 11.1.28 (Lewis & Short)

    Post-Augustan (Seneca, Quintilian, Pliny), as Lewis & Short marks it.

Examples

  • est enim quātenus amīcitiae darī venia possit

    for there is a point up to which friendship may be indulgedCic. Lael. 61

  • nēmō adeō ferus est, ut nōn mītēscere possit, sī modo cultūrae patientem commodet aurem

    no one is so wild that he cannot be tamed, if only he lends a patient ear to trainingHor. Ep. 1.1.39–40

  • Aliquātenus, inquis, dolēre, aliquātenus timēre permitte

    “Allow me to grieve to some extent,” you say, “and to fear to some extent”Sen. Ep. 116.3

See also how far is it?, far.

Citations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j).
